Since the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been an awareness of the need to develop data management for healthcare because it can produce a rapid response to the COVID-19 outbreak based on healthcare data. As biological, social, and environmental crises, pandemics require science models to anticipate, predict, and respond [1]. Health data exchange between health facilities is fast becoming increasingly dependent on interoperability because data analysis from multiple sources within a hospital, combined with data from other hospitals and public databases, can provide critical insights into disease mechanisms for diagnosis, prognosis, and intervention [2]. Scientific knowledge exchange is also enabled by data interoperability among scientists worldwide. The COVID-19 clinical use case illustrates how crucial interoperability is for broader public health [3].
Ideally, hospital systems should be designed with integrative, federated data analytics. Global data scientists have proposed that this can be accomplished by implementing agreed-upon standards to make data globally findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable for humans and computers, also known as "the FAIR principles" [2]. "The FAIR principles are as follows: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable, intending to make digital objects human and machine-readable. The principles establish several standards for manual and automated filing, retrieval, sharing, and reuse in modern media environments [4]. Several projects support the FAIR data principles in their data management strategies, such as the GO-FAIR Virus Outbreak Data Network (VODAN), the ZonMW Covid program, the Trusted World of Corona (TWOC), and the ELIXIR COVID project. VODAN-Africa, one of the VODAN project implementation networks, was inspired by the experience of Ebola to establish COVID-19 FAIR Data Points (FDP) in African countries and to make Africa a huge data source on the COVID-19 pandemic [5]. This project involved Leiden University Medical Centre (LUMC) and several African countries, including Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, Liberia, Somalia, and Tunisia, to support analytics at the point of care through the development of an architecture for recording clinical health data and research data about COVID-19, which are produced as human- and machine-readable data objects in a distributed architecture of locally governed, linked, human- and machine-readable data [6]. 
The widespread adoption and application of the FAIR principles concept, as well as rapid technological advancements that could lead to rapid scientific advancements, pose challenges for protecting personal data. Digital health implementation has many meaningful applications, but high dependence on sensitive information concerning patients' health can inevitably trigger data security problems [7]. New obligations on the protection of natural persons concerning the processing of personal data have been added since the new European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) came into force in May 2018. The GDPR will be a game changer for digital health by requiring the health organizations that implement digital health practices to protect patients' data by following the regulations to ensure individual confidence. The GDPR force security aspects of personal data must be enhanced and significantly impact governments and businesses. Existing systems and data flows may have to be modified to comply with the new rules and limitations [8]. Consequently, to minimize liability under the GDPR, organizations worldwide need to make changes to comply with the regulation [9]. 
FAIR-based data management strategies have been proposed to improve the standards for patient data generation and interoperability by using data localization strategies, and GDPR was used as a baseline standard to bridge the governance gap, which resulted in the implementation of two studies in Africa from April 2020 to September 2020 and October 2020 to October 2021 [9]. In contrast to earlier development, however, several gaps arise in the data protection objective for the project. Even though the GDPR is the golden standard of data protection regulation globally [10], it needs a comparison with the local regulation applied in VODAN-Africa country members since the differences in the data protection regulation could affect how data protection is implemented in each country. Moreover, the VODAN-Africa implementation would have been more accurate if it had included the stakeholder perspective on data protection, such as the health facilities personnel, the country coordinators' leader, and the Government that supports the project. Finally, assessing the VODAN-Africa architecture with the GDPR and the local data protection regulation compliance is crucial to show that VODAN-Africa is not only want to improve data ownership but also trustable in holding patients’ data; therefore, it could increase trust for the stakeholder involved in VODAN-Africa.
This research investigates the basis of data protection development of FAIR-based health system deployment in the VODAN project from the perspective of the Three Pillars Cyber Security model [11]: People, Process, and Technology (PPT) Framework. PPT (people, process, and technology) is a method to drive action by balancing people, processes, and technology: People perform a specific type of work for an organization by following processes (and often using technology) to streamline and improve their work. An organization can benefit from this framework when deciding whether to purchase or implement new technology to achieve harmony within the organization. In the FAIR implementation within the VODAN-Africa, the people refer to the VODAN-Africa members on patients' data protection within their related environment. The process is about the current condition of the data protection in the data flow within the health facilities and the comparison between the local regulation and the GDPR to identify compliance. Lastly, the technology refers to the assessment of privacy by a design approach that embeds in development of the VODAN-Africa architecture.

Sub ExtractData()
 ' Declare variables
 Dim MyFolder As String
 Dim MyFile As String
 Dim SourceWB As Workbook
 Dim SourceWS As Worksheet
 Dim DestWB As Workbook
 Dim DestWS As Worksheet
 Dim NextRow As Long
 Dim LastRow As Long
 
 ' Set the folder path containing the source files
 MyFolder = ThisWorkbook.Path & "\input\"
 
 ' Set the destination workbook and worksheet
 Set DestWB = ThisWorkbook
 Set DestWS = DestWB.Sheets("SOFUN")
 
 ' Find the next empty cell in column B of the destination worksheet
 LastRow = DestWS.Cells(DestWS.Rows.Count, "B").End(xlUp).Row
 If LastRow = 1 And IsEmpty(DestWS.Cells(1, "B")) Then
 NextRow = 1
 Else
 NextRow = LastRow + 1
 End If
 
 ' Loop through each file in the folder
 MyFile = Dir(MyFolder & "\*.xlsx")
 Do While MyFile <> ""
 ' Open the source workbook
 Set SourceWB = Workbooks.Open(MyFolder & MyFile)
 
 ' Set the source worksheet
 Set SourceWS = SourceWB.Sheets("Settings")
 
 ' Extract the data and copy to the destination worksheet
 DestWS.Cells(NextRow, "B").Value = SourceWS.Range("B2").Value
 DestWS.Cells(NextRow, "C").Value = SourceWS.Range("C2").Value
 DestWS.Cells(NextRow, "D").Value = SourceWS.Range("D2").Value
 DestWS.Cells(NextRow, "E").Value = SourceWS.Range("E2").Value
 
 ' Close the source workbook without saving changes
 SourceWB.Close False
 
 ' Move to the next row in the destination worksheet
 NextRow = NextRow + 1
 
 ' Move to the next file in the folder
 MyFile = Dir
 Loop
 
 ' Display a message box when the extraction is complete
 MsgBox "Data extraction is complete!", vbInformation, "Complete"
End Sub

environment for a number of reasons. Firstly, unlike many terrestrial animals, fish do
not have vocal cords and instead use internal mechanical sound e.g through rubbing
together of bones or vibrating the swim bladder with sonic muscles – this means that
there they can have little to no obvious external movement when the vocalisations

we have in place to identify the direction a sound is coming from does not work for
us in the water. Therefore, we can hear fish vocalisations whilst in the water, but we
find it hard to pinpoint where they are coming from, making it hard to know which fish
is making which sound. In short, is it very hard to identify fish vocalisations by just

stereo directional hearing apparatus using directional hydrophones and wet

CHAPTER EIGHT
 The Insurance Game
 From Chris
This is an “aside” from our main thesis, but an important one. There is an “insurance game” that plays a part in the lives of almost all of us with back pain, and the game is fixed . . . against us. One of our goals in doing this book is to cut you loose from its tangles—because insurance today is structured to push you to do repetitive and ultimately useless fixes (not cures), and it sometimes it pushes you in the wrong (read “dangerous”) direction. 
Most insurers are not wonderfully straight in their dealings with certain aspects of back pain. I am not talking so much here about medical events; they are a little different. I am talking about the use of therapists and other healers, whom so many of you spend so much on. 
Here is the problem. Most insurers pay for some therapeutic treatment of back pain, but the payments (like most therapies and therapists) are focused on fixes, not cures. For example, insurers pay (about $50 a treatment) for a chiropractor to do an “adjustment” of your back (i.e., he or she will “pop” your back with a high-velocity treatment of the spine or joint). A little bit of history may help here. It was once believed that when chiropractors did high-velocity treatments (i.e., “popped” your spine), they were actually straightening out a “kink.” That is, you had somehow “thrown out” your back, and the chiropractor, God bless him, straightened it out again. Sounded great and, sure enough, you got some relief. Alas, that’s not usually what happens, and the relief was temporary.
When chiropractors “pop” your back with the application of high-velocity manipulation (and there often is a pop), what they really are doing, in most cases, is restoring range of motion to a joint and/or releasing a muscle spasm. That pop you hear is the release of gases that build up in the joint. Restoring range of motion and releasing a spasm is a blessed relief, often enough, but it has nothing to do with curing the condition that caused the spasm in the first place. So, absent any further instructions from the therapist about behavior change, we are talking a purely palliative step. 
But most insurers see additional chiropractic treatment (e.g., instruction about exercise and other behavior), which might really do some good, as just an incidental “add-on” and pay only some $10 a patient for it. For most chiropractors that won’t pay the bills. Better for them to do a bunch of adjustments (or pops) and give their patients blessed relief and stay in business to help their patients another day. So even assuming that the chiropractor knows how to address serious back pain for the long haul, he or she is not really compensated to try. 
The story is similarly wrong-headed but a little different with physical therapists. Therapists are paid to do exercise, but the payment model almost assures that they go at it in a way that is not as useful as it could be. Basically, insurers will pay for treating only functional limitations. That means things like being unable to sleep, turn over in bed, put on your clothes. Beyond that, you are on your own. You can’t ski or jog or play with the kids? Tough . . . not covered. And your back still hurts like crazy all the time? Still no insurance. Insurance pays for only the minimum level of functionality. Therapists are not paid to analyze how you got in this jam in the first place, they are not paid to teach you how to avoid future incidents, and they are not paid to set you on a course of serious strength training of the kind that we talk about in this book, which is the only thing that is likely to effect a permanent cure, even assuming that they know how to do so. 
To make things worse, many of the outcome measures mandated by insurers (to determine whether you have been returned to the minimal level of functionality) are outdated and even dangerous. In particular, the insurers often place great emphasis on range of motion of the lumbar spine. In Jeremy’s view, this is the least important measure of change in most cases and may be counterproductive. The goal of sound treatment is not a more flexible lower spine; it is teaching the patient stability. So measuring recovery in terms of the flexibility of the lumbar spine is usually wrong. And urges you—and your practitioner—to try to do things you should not be doing.
